voiceover: How can a bridge move while hundreds of ants are walking over it?
visual_direction: Forest-floor gap, linked-ant bridge, nestmates crossing; slow push-in

voiceover: Some army ants build living roadways by linking their bodies across gaps in the forest floor.
visual_direction: Macro view of linked workers and traffic; anatomically plausible ants

voiceover: Their nestmates stream over the structure instead of following a longer detour.
visual_direction: Overhead winding route contrasted with direct bridge crossing

voiceover: But the bridge keeps changing. In field experiments with Eciton hamatum, researchers watched bridges lengthen, widen and shift toward the main trail.
visual_direction: Before/after positions; workers join and leave; gap geometry consistent

voiceover: The movement increased when traffic was heavier. The likely mechanism is local: workers in busier sections are more likely to be joined by passing ants,
visual_direction: Busier side receives more contacts; workers attach; label as likely mechanism

voiceover: while less-contacted workers are more likely to leave. No ant needs to know the whole route.
visual_direction: Low-contact edge loses workers while busy side gains them

voiceover: The shortcut saves travel, but every ant holding the bridge is temporarily unavailable for foraging. So the structure settles where the colony's traffic benefit is balanced against the workers it ties up.
